results.title: EOD: Enabling Low Latency GNN Inference via Near-Memory Concatenate Aggregation | Proceedings of the 52nd Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture
results.content: In this setup, the system must prepare the computational graph and input node features for target nodes, followed by GNN inference using the given input data. Once these data are prepared, the next step is transferring them to the accelerator device, such as GPUs. Finally, the accelerator device computes the GNN model for the target node batches and returns the inference outputs. Leveraging precomputed train nodes, we design a DIMM-based Near-Memory Processing (NMP) architecture to accelerate train-to-target aggregation. We propose a preprocessing method for inductive GNN inference serving, which includes train node precomputation and feature vector concatenated ZVC compression. However, in the context of GNN-based real-time services, where results for a small number of unseen target nodes are frequently requested, the redundant computations in full-batch inference become excessive. **1) Preparation:** : Before computing the GNN models to acquire the inference result, two types of input data must be prepared: the computational graph and the feature vectors of input nodes for the first layer of the GNN. However, neighborhood explosion becomes a primary factor contributing to increased latency during mini-batch inference, primarily due to the propagation among train (*tr*) nodes caused by the multi-layer nature of GNNs. This propagation must be computed for each target (*tar*) node batch request, as omitting it significantly degrades accuracy [51]. Figure 4(b) illustrates the process where target nodes use off-line precomputed hidden features to compute only with 1-hop neighbor nodes *L* times, resulting in the final output. While this approach reduces memory access and speeds up for the real-time inference, this incurs a *L* times capacity overhead because precomputed hidden features of train nodes need to be stored in memory. Figure 7 shows the capacity requirements for the training data to be prepared before inference with ZVC and adjusted ReLU thresholds, based on results from the commonly used 2-4 layers in GNNs. The baseline consists of the train input feature and tr-to-tr edge, which derives results using these two components. In practical deployments, such latencies significantly affect the real-time performance of GNN inference pipelines, especially in scenarios with high query throughput or large-scale graph data distributed across multiple nodes.

results.title: LLM Inference – Optimizing Latency, Throughput, and Scalability – Victor Leung
results.content:
Title: LLM Inference – Optimizing Latency, Throughput, and Scalability – Victor Leung
# LLM Inference – Optimizing Latency, Throughput, and Scalability. Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) for inference is a complex yet rewarding process that requires balancing performance, cost, and scalability. Optimizing and sizing LLM inference systems involves understanding tradeoffs, selecting the right tools, and leveraging NVIDIA’s advanced technologies like TensorRT-LLM, Triton Inference Server, and NVIDIA Inference Microservices (NIM). One of the most critical considerations in LLM inference is the tradeoff between latency and throughput. By relaxing latency requirements, you can significantly boost throughput and reduce Total Cost of Ownership (TCO). TP2 improves latency for individual requests but incurs communication overhead between GPUs. For optimal performance, consider using NVLink-enabled servers like DGX or HGX systems or PCIe-connected H100 NVL cards. This makes FP8 especially useful for large-scale deployments where reducing memory usage and maximizing throughput are critical. TensorRT-LLM optimizes models for specific hardware constraints like latency or throughput, while Triton Inference Server simplifies deployment with features like dynamic batching and multi-framework support. For models larger than 13B parameters, use NVLink-enabled systems to handle increased memory requirements and inter-GPU communication efficiently. Streaming mode prioritizes Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) for real-time applications like chatbots, while sequential mode optimizes End-to-End Latency (E2E) for tasks requiring complete responses before consumption. Strict latency limits reduce throughput but may be necessary for certain real-time applications. While cloud APIs simplify deployment, they provide less control over latency and throughput compared to on-prem solutions. In-Flight Batching (IFB) dynamically combines requests at different stages (prefill and decoding) into a single batch, maintaining nearly constant batch sizes for higher GPU utilization while reducing latency by allowing new requests to enter ongoing batches without waiting for current ones to complete. Sizing LLM inference systems involves navigating tradeoffs between latency, throughput, hardware constraints, and deployment costs. By leveraging NVIDIA’s advanced tools like TensorRT-LLM and NIM alongside optimization techniques such as tensor parallelism, IFB, and precision scaling (FP8), you can deploy scalable and efficient inference systems tailored to your application’s requirements. Whether you’re building real-time chatbots or processing large-scale datasets offline, these best practices will help you design robust AI-powered solutions that balance performance with cost-effectiveness! * Share on LinkedIn (Opens in new window) LinkedIn. results.title: Inductive Link Prediction in Knowledge Graphs
results.content:
Title: Inductive Link Prediction in Knowledge Graphs
Inductive Link Prediction in Knowledge Graphs | by Michael Galkin | TDS Archive | Medium. Inductive Link Prediction in Knowledge Graphs. Starting a new Inductive Link Prediction Challenge 2022. Since very 2011, the area of representation learning over Knowledge Graphs has been dominated by one task: transductive link prediction. Inductive: inference is on the new graph. In the **transductive** setup (🖼 ☝️) we perform inference (our link prediction) over the **same** graph seen at training time. With the growth of graphs in industry (100M to 10B+ nodes) and enormous computational costs of re-training every time a graph has changed, the focus of KG representation learning is moving towards **inductive** models that are free from the above limitations. Instead, most of the progress in representation learning in 2021–2022 (like **Neural Bellman-Ford Networks** or **NodePiece**) is achieved either on new KG modalities (like hyper-relational KGs) or having **inductive** properties in mind 👉 check out our recent article on the Graph ML State of Affairs in KGs for more details. In the **inductive** setup, we lift off the requirement of having the same graph at training and inference time. 1.   **Fully-Inductive**: a new graph totally disconnected from the training one. Fully-inductive setup — an inference graph is disconnected from the training one. Semi-inductive setup: an inference graph extends the training one with new nodes (orange). Inductive models pose an additional **representation learning** challenge, i.e., we can’t use shallow vector assignment per node anymore and we need more efficient ways to construct node features that will be able to generalize to new unseen nodes. Inductive Link Prediction Challenge 2022. 🐍 In Team PyKEEN, we designed a new Inductive Link Prediction Challenge (ILPC) aimed at consolidating community efforts in creating inductive reasoning models. For 2022, we propose the inductive link prediction challenge in the **fully-inductive** mode, i.e., when training and inference graphs are disjoint. *   Finally, ILPC releases together with the new PyKEEN 1.8.0 version featuring inductive link prediction pipelines, new interfaces to build inductive models, and many new evaluation metrics 📏. A new and open Inductive Link Prediction Challenge 2022 has started, try your best GNNs and other architectures!

results.title: Inductive Link Prediction — pykeen 1.11.1 documentation
results.content:
Title: Inductive Link Prediction — pykeen 1.11.1 documentation
* An inference graph is totally disconnected from the training graph (disjoint), aka *fully-inductive* setup.Link prediction pattern between entities is therefore *unseen-to-unseen*. It is supposed to contain more than 3 triple factories, i.e., in the *fully-inductive* setup it is expected to have at least 4 triple factories (transductive\_training, inductive\_inference, inductive\_validation, inductive\_test). transductive\_training is the graph with entities index (0..N) on which we will train a model, inductive\_inference is the new graph appearing at inference time with new entities (indexing (0..K)). inductive\_validation and inductive\_test share the entities with inductive\_inference but not with transductive\_training. This way, we inform a model that we are predicting links against the inductive inference graph, not against the training graph. PyKEEN supports 12 fully-inductive datasets introduced by  where training and inductive inference graphs are disjoint. """Setup an inductive node piece model with GNN encoder.""" from  pykeen.datasets.inductive.ilp_teru  import InductiveFB15k237 from  pykeen.losses  import NSSALoss from  pykeen.models.inductive  import InductiveNodePieceGNN dataset = InductiveFB15k237(version = "v1", create_inverse_triples = True) model = InductiveNodePieceGNN(triples_factory = dataset. When set to mode=”training”, an inductive model has to invoke representations of the training graph, when set to mode=validation or mode=testing, the model has to invoke representations of inference graphs. """Train the inductive model.""" from  pykeen.datasets.inductive.ilp_teru  import InductiveFB15k237 from  pykeen.evaluation.rank_based_evaluator  import SampledRankBasedEvaluator from  pykeen.training  import SLCWATrainingLoop dataset = InductiveFB15k237(version = "v1", create_inverse_triples = True) model =...# model init here, one of InductiveNodePiece optimizer =... mapped_triples, # filter out true inference triples) test_evaluator = SampledRankBasedEvaluator(mode = "testing",# necessary to specify for the inductive mode - this will use inference nodes evaluation_factory = dataset. mapped_triples, # filter out true inference triples).
